title: From a Python install to an Apple stock chart

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Here's a test for any beginner workshop. Every new idea should have somewhere to go. If it doesn't, people forget it by the next slide.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like most tutorials I've sat through. Lots of concepts, no destination.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. So Antoine wrote about AlgoETS Workshop one, a teaching repository that does the opposite. It starts with Python setup, moves to an API response, then a data frame, then a chart. Everything feeds the next step.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nine Jupyter notebooks in six numbered folders. Two for setup, two for Python, one for APIs, one for pandas, two for visualization, and a final project. Antoine is careful to say that's a count of teaching material, not a number of students who finished.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Fair. And setup is usually where beginners give up, isn't it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is, so the repo offers a Colab link and a local Jupyter install. People can start writing code right away, and treat environment setup as its own topic later. The numbered folders also mean you can go back to one missing concept without redoing the whole project.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What's the payoff at the end?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The final notebook plots Apple closing prices with exponential moving averages. Twelve, twenty-six, fifty, a hundred and two hundred days. It ties together the request, the table, the indicator columns and a labeled chart.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So is this a trading strategy?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No, and the post says so plainly. It doesn't show that any crossover makes money. It's a data exercise.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What would you ask a class looking at that chart?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Technical things. Are the dates in order? Were missing values removed on purpose? Why does a longer average react more slowly? Are all the curves computed from the same observations?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Any warning before someone tries it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. APIs, keys and package versions may have changed since the original workshop. Treat the notebooks as material to read and adapt, not a one-command setup.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And where does it lead next?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: To Antoine's batch backtesting engine. Same indicator idea, tested across many instruments with recorded assumptions. The point is understanding data and code before trusting any leaderboard. The full post has the flow diagram and the links to each notebook.
